items_missed: Never asked 'how are you today?' and never set an agenda. The call opened with the customer's request and Calvin's very next words were 'Okay, what's the square footage on your home?' — no greeting exchange, no roadmap, no timeframe, no 'sound good?'. This is a caller who told him within sixty seconds that he is older and uncomfortable with technology; he was the customer on this board who most needed to be told what was about to happen.

Availability was never checked or mentioned. The customer said 'between now before Thanksgiving' and Calvin answered 'Okay. So it's probably sometime in October or September. Okay. So pretty wide range.' He never said Einstein has open dates in that window, never named one, and never gave the customer a reason to move off 'sometime.'

Origin address never captured. He got the destination zip (77515) because the customer volunteered it, then asked 'you don't have an address yet in, in the, at the unload' — but the San Antonio pickup address, the thing that determines the trip fee he then quoted at $1,056, was never asked for.
Stairs and floors never asked at either end, on a three-bedroom, 1,520 sq ft home going interstate.
Special considerations — long walks, narrow hallways, tight turns — never asked.

Storage stops, additional stops, and access concerns (parking, driveway, elevator, HOA) all never asked. On a three-day move with an overnight hotel leg, access at the far end is a schedule risk, and the far-end address does not even exist yet.

The moving-stressor question was never asked, and the customer handed him the stressor out loud: 'I just don't feel I'm that adapted all this new electronic stuff I'm old.' Calvin handled it kindly but never converted it into 'what are you most worried about with this move?' — which on a solo interstate move to a son's town is where the real objection lives.

No hourly rate was ever stated. This is the central failure of the call. Einstein sells time, and the customer came off the phone knowing exactly three numbers — $240 overnight fee, $1,056 trip fee, about $300 in packing materials — and not one of them is the rate. He was quoted $1,596 of accessorial charges and zero dollars of actual moving service.
No 'pricing is super simple' opener, and structurally the opposite happened: the fee stack came first and the rate never came at all.
What's-included list was thin: 'the pads and wrap are included insurance and all the items is included.' No gas, no truck, no taxes, no tools, no bands.

No Worries Damage Coverage was named but not explained: 'it's all fully insured including higher evaluation, no worries, damage coverage that we provide in our hourly rate just to give peace of mind our clients.' The brand name landed; the $2,000, the 'repair, replace, or reimburse,' and the 60¢/lb industry baseline all did not — and 60¢/lb on a three-day interstate move is exactly the comparison that makes this differentiator worth money.
Meet Your Mover never mentioned.
On-Time Guarantee never mentioned.

No 'no hidden fees' pitch, on the one call in this batch where it was most needed. He read out $240 + $1,056 + $300 with no framing around them, so from the customer's side the call sounded like a list of surcharges. 'No credit card fees, no fuel surcharge, no assembly fees — the overnight and the trip fee are the only two additions and here is exactly what each one covers' would have reframed the same numbers entirely.

Clock start and the 2.5 hour minimum were both never mentioned. Fifteen-minute proration was covered twice and well ('you do only pay for what we use and we do bill in fifteen minute increments on each day so you only pay for the time that's needed') but there is no floor and no start point attached to it.
No sense-check at any point in the pricing or structure explanation, on a call with a customer who had already told him he struggles to follow new information.

No estimate was given. No hours per day, no total, no range, no dollar figure of any kind for the actual move. The customer asked for a quote in his opening sentence — 'Give me a quote on moving my stuff' — and eight minutes later he has a promise of one by 3:00 instead.

No typical time range for a 1,520 sq ft three-bedroom, and no mover or truck count. He referenced having quoted a near-identical job — 'that's funny, I kinda just quoted a move. Pretty similar, same square footage going to San Angelo' — and then did not use a single number from it.
Specialty items never asked. Piano, safe, gun safe, antiques, appliances — none of it, on a 1,520 sq ft three-bedroom being packed and hauled 250 miles.
Walk distance never asked; no equivalents used to make the three-day structure feel concrete.

Save Your Ass speech entirely absent — 0/10. The customer is buying a full pack, which makes reps assume the speech does not apply. It applies more: every item he pre-consolidates is a box Einstein does not have to pack, on a day that is being billed hourly. 'Anything you can get into a tub or a corner before we get there, we pack around it faster, and that comes off day one' is a direct dollar saving on a three-day job.

No booking attempt and no date-holding attempt. A wide-open window ('between now before Thanksgiving') is not a reason to skip the ask; it is a reason to make it — 'let me put a soft hold on a week in October so you are not competing with everyone else's end-of-month.'

No deposit required never mentioned. On a ~$5,000-plus interstate job with a customer who has not picked a destination address yet, 'it costs nothing to hold a date and there is no card on file' is the single lowest-friction way to get commitment out of an undecided caller.

No bolded-details framing on the email, no business hours, no phone number, and no 'any other questions before I let you go?' The close was 'we'll just keep, keep in touch' — which, for a caller who just told him he is not good with technology, leaves the entire next step resting on an email he may or may not open.
Customer's name used once. He got it late and awkwardly — 'What did you said your name was Alvin?' — after the customer had already given it in his opening line, 'my name's Alvin fen.'
top_strength: Calvin's handling of the technology objection is the best emotional read on this board. The customer said 'I just don't feel I'm that adapted all this new electronic stuff I'm old,' which is the kind of line that makes most reps abandon the virtual walkthrough and move on. Calvin did neither — he stayed with it, lowered the stakes with a concrete question rather than reassurance ('Gotcha, it's. Do you have a cell? I mean, you have a cellphone'), and then described the mechanism in one sentence so the customer could picture it: 'usually you just get a link and we just send a link to the phone, you get it as a text and then when you click the link you can join the video call. It is pretty easy.' When the customer still hesitated, he normalized it without pushing — 'we do have obviously, you know people clients that aren't that tech savvy and we work with them. And you know they does kind of come somewhat naturally sometimes cause it's not super difficult' — and then gave him three graded ways in: inventory list, photos, or the video call. That is a rep meeting an objection by widening the path instead of arguing. His second strength is structural clarity on a genuinely complicated job. He built the three-day shape out loud, in order, before being asked: 'so it'd be three days actually so we would come in and pack a box, pack everything in the boxes, probably prep the furniture with pads and wrap on that day, day two we would load everything into our truck. We were drive to what was it Richwood or 77515 we would stay overnight and then nearby hotel and then on day three we would unload everything and then we would drive back to San antonio.' He also explained the trip fee by what it actually pays for rather than asserting it — 'a trip fee that would cover the empty truck driving back after the unload on day three' — and he gave a real box-count benchmark and invited the customer to test it against his own house: 'for how home that size typically we're gonna end up packing about fifty to sixty boxes. So, I don't know if that sounds like it'll be about right for you.' Finally, he committed to a specific delivery time on the follow-up — 'I'll get you an email here probably before 3:00' — which is a small thing most reps skip and the only hard commitment anywhere in this call.
coaching_note: Highest-leverage fix: Calvin quoted every fee and never quoted the service. Run the numbers the customer actually received — $240 overnight, $1,056 trip fee, roughly $300 in materials — and then note what is missing: the hourly rate, the crew size, the truck count, the hours per day, and any total. He sold a 1,520 sq ft three-day interstate move and the caller cannot say within $3,000 what it costs. This inverts the entire pricing structure in the customer's head: instead of 'a simple hourly rate, with two additions for the distance,' he heard 'a pile of fees.' The sequence has to flip, every time: rate first, what it includes second, the two long-distance additions third, then the estimate. Second priority: he had the comparable and did not use it. 'I kinda just quoted a move. Pretty similar, same square footage going to San Angelo' is the single most useful sentence available to him on this call, and it produced no number. He should have said: 'I quoted almost exactly this last week — same square footage, similar distance — and it ran about X hours on the pack day and Y on the load, which put them around $Z all in. Yours should land close to that, and the inventory list will tell me if I need to adjust.' That converts a wide-open call into a real anchor and gives the customer something to react to. Third: no ask of any kind. No date held, no soft booking, no deposit line, no follow-up call scheduled. The customer said 'between now before Thanksgiving' and the entire next step is an email plus a hope. Put a specific follow-up on the calendar out loud — 'I'll send this before three; can I call you Tuesday morning to walk through it together?' — which also solves the tech-comfort problem, because a phone walkthrough is the format this particular customer is actually comfortable with. Fourth: he confirmed the email address, then lost it, then asked again mid-call ('And what was your email address? Okay, I got that. Sorry'), and never read it back for confirmation. On a call where the entire outcome depends on an email arriving, read it back. Finally, the Save Your Ass speech is a zero and should not be. Full-pack jobs are where reps assume it does not apply, and it is where the hourly savings are largest — every pre-consolidated corner shortens a day that is being billed at an hourly rate the customer was never even told.
phone_presence_notes: Real warmth shows up exactly once, on the technology objection, where he stayed patient and normalized it ('we do have obviously, you know people clients that aren't that tech savvy and we work with them'), and there is a small genuine moment in 'that's funny, I kinda just quoted a move. Pretty similar' — but the rest is transactional and halting, with the customer's name used once, no warm-up, no empathy markers, and the email address asked for twice ('And what was your email address? Okay, I got that. Sorry').
audio_review_reason: The speaking-clearly bonus point was deducted on transcript evidence that is genuinely ambiguous. The delivery shows repeated stalls and self-interruptions — 'What I can do?', 'So I don't know yeah, how save you are', 'I guess tar rough, rough kind of timeframe' — which could be a rep thinking out loud on a complicated interstate job, a bad line, or transcription artifact. Audio would also settle whether the customer, who described himself as older and struggling with technology, was actually following the fee stack or just being polite.
